To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the left ventricular geometry was normal in the majority of patients with adult-onset growth hormone deficiency (about 75% of patients), but 25% of them showed high left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) consisting of eccentric remodeling, not dissimilarly from overweight controls.

(1) the majority of patients had low LVM, but about one-fourth of them showed high LVM/LVM index; (2) the main LV geometric pattern is eccentric hypertrophy, not dissimilarly from controls; (3) this finding is worthy to be confirmed in GHD patients with wider controlled trials.
about 25% GHD patients showed subclinical left ventricle hypertrophy, not dissimilarly from overweight controls, but with a different pathophysiological mechanism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a BMI-independent role of GH in LV remodeling, which is worthy to be studied further.
a possible subclinical LV remodeling in GHD patients, which may be a consequence of a complex interplay of hormonal, hemodynamic, and metabolic factors.
a BMI-independent effect of GHD on LV remodeling.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the absence of other risk factors, adult-onset GGD does not seem to be associated with increased LV mass and/or abnormal LV geometric remodeling.
, in GHD patients, a high LVMi is not BMI dependent and it is not a mere consequence of overweight.
GHD is a condition that, even if associated with high BMI, may be associated to subclinical left ventricle eccentric hypertrophy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, despite a normal resting cardiac morphology, about one quarter of GHD patients may have an increased LV mass index, which could be a sign of early subclinical cardiac dysfunction.
GHD patients, though having a low BMI, have a high prevalence of LV eccentric hypertrophy, not dissimilarly from overweight controls.
the LV geometric remodeling is a BMI-independent feature of adult-onset GHRD, which is worthy to be further investigated in larger cohorts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the GHD-related high LVMi is not BMI-dependent.
GHD patients should be carefully monitored for cardiovascular risk, even in the presence of normal body weight.

GHD patients with high LVMi may have a different cardiovascular risk profile, and that the presence of subclinical LV eccentric hypertrophy should be considered as a potential risk factor for cardiovascular events.
